english: I save 500,000 won each month.
tip: Money uses Sino numbers: 오십만 원 (osimman won) = 500,000 won.

english: My card bill came out high this month.
tip: Bills 'come out' in Korean: 카드값이 이번 달에 많이 나왔어요 (kadeugapsi ibeon dare mani nawasseoyo) = the card bill came out high this month. 나오다 (naoda = come out) is how charges show up.

english: I swiped my card way too much.
tip: 긁다 (geukda) literally means 'scratch' – Korean pictures card spending as scratching the card: 카드를 긁었어요 (kadeureul geulgeosseoyo) = I swiped my card.

english: I find cards more convenient than cash.
tip: -보다 = than: 현금보다 (hyeongeumboda) = than cash.

english: A transfer fee was added.
tip: Fees stick on in Korean: 수수료가 붙었어요 (susuryoga buteosseoyo) uses 붙다 (butda) 'stick' – the fee attached itself to the transfer.

english: I called the bank and cancelled it.
tip: -아/어서 = and then: 전화해서 (jeonhwahaeseo) = called, and then...

english: There's a set withdrawal limit.
tip: 정해져 있어요 (jeonghaejyeo isseoyo) uses -아/어 있어요 (-a/eo isseoyo) for a state that was set and stays set – the limit isn't being set now, it already sits there fixed.

english: I have to pay interest every month.
tip: -아/어야 해요 (-a/eoya haeyo) means 'have to': 내야 해요 (naeya haeyo) = must pay. Literally 'only if you pay does it work' – obligation built from a condition.

english: I borrowed money from a friend.
tip: -한테 usually means 'to', but with 빌렸어요 (billyeosseoyo = borrowed) it flips to 'from': 친구한테 (chinguhante) = from a friend. The verb decides the direction.

english: I'll definitely pay it back next month.
tip: -(으)ㄹ게요 = I promise to: 갚을게요 (gapeulgeyo) = I'll pay it back.

english: If you take a loan, interest builds up.
tip: -(으)면 = if: 받으면 (badeumyeon) = if you take/receive it.

english: I'm looking for a bank with low interest.
tip: A whole clause can sit before a noun: 이자가 낮은 은행 (ijaga najeun eunhaeng) = 'interest-is-low bank' – Korean front-loads the description English puts after.

english: My spending is more than my income.
tip: -보다 (-boda) marks the compared thing and 더 (deo) spells out 'more': 수입보다 지출이 더 많아요 (suip-boda jichuri deo manayo) = spending exceeds income. 더 is optional but adds punch.

english: Living costs are high.
tip: Costs go in, in Korean: 들다 (deulda) 'enter' is the cost verb – 생활비가 많이 들어요 (saenghwalbiga mani deureoyo) = living costs 'go in' a lot, i.e. they're high.

english: I mustn't go over budget.
tip: -(으)면 안 돼요 = must not: 넘으면 안 돼요 (neomeumyeon an dwaeyo).

english: I try to buy only what I need.
tip: -(으)려고 해요 = intend to: 사려고 해요 (saryeogo haeyo) = plan to buy.

english: The kids' education costs are really high.
tip: Korean costs 'enter': 교육비가 정말 많이 들어요 (gyoyukbiga jeongmal mani deureoyo) = education really costs a lot, literally 'education money enters'. 들다 (deulda), no separate verb 'to cost'.

english: My husband and I keep the ledger together.
tip: -(이)랑 = with: 남편이랑 (nampyeon-irang) = with my husband.

english: Saving has become a habit now.
tip: What you become takes 이/가 (i/ga), not an object marker: 습관이 됐어요 (seupgwani dwaesseoyo) = became a habit. With 되다 (doeda), the result acts like a subject.

target: 제 목표는 빚을 다 갚는 거예요.
english: My goal is to pay off all my debt.
tip: 갚는 거예요 (gamneun geoyeyo) wraps the verb in -는 거 (-neun geo) = 'the act of paying off' – how Korean states a goal: my goal IS the paying-off, a noun-like thing.

english: I want to spend money wisely.
tip: 현명하게 (hyeonmyeonghage) = wisely; -게 makes an adverb.

english: I enrolled in university this semester.
tip: 입학하다 (iphakada = to enroll) takes 에: 대학교에 입학해요 (daehakgyoe iphakaeyo).

target: 첫 수업이 아침 아홉 시에 시작해요.
english: The first class starts at nine in the morning.
tip: 시 (si = o'clock) takes native numbers: 아홉 시 (ahop si = nine o'clock).

english: The professor makes their lectures really interesting.
tip: 께서 (kkeseo) marks an honored subject and pairs with -세요: 교수님께서 하세요 (gyosunimkkeseo haseyo).

english: My sibling's lecture room is on the third floor.
tip: 층 (cheung = floor) uses Sino numbers: 삼 층 (sam cheung = 3rd floor).

english: I major in business administration.
tip: 전공하다 (jeongonghada = to major) takes 을/를: 경영학을 전공해요 (gyeongyeonghageul jeongonghaeyo).

english: My major is computer engineering.
tip: 이에요/예요 = 'is': after a consonant 공학이에요 (gonghagieyo); after a vowel 친구예요 (chinguyeyo).

english: I'm taking six courses this semester.
tip: 과목 (gwamok = course) counts with native numbers: 여섯 과목 (yeoseot gwamok = six courses).

english: I have as many as three classes today.
tip: -이나 (-ina) means 'as many as': 세 개나 (se gaena = as many as three).

english: I share my dorm room with a roommate.
tip: 하고 (hago = with) joins people: 룸메이트하고 (rummeiteuhago = with a roommate).
